speaker: Doctor
text:
Can you describe exactly what happens during these episodes of unresponsiveness, and how long do they typically last?

REQUEST TEST: EEG

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Interictal spikes and sharp waves localized to the temporal lobes, more prominent on the right side.

speaker: Patient
text: 7-year-old boy. The patient has been experiencing recurrent episodes lasting 3–4 minutes each of facial grimacing and staring over the past month. During these episodes, he is nonresponsive and does not recall them afterward. He reports a muddy taste in his mouth before the onset of these episodes. His brother witnessed him waking up, staring, and making hand gestures during one episode. The patient felt lethargic and confused afterwards.

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: No significant previous medical history. No prior seizures or neurological evaluations. Social history: Enrolled in second grade. Lives with parents and one sibling. No reported use of medications or exposure to toxins.

speaker: Patient
text: Denies fever, headache, visual or auditory disturbances, weakness, or other systemic symptoms. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Multiple sclerosis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text:
That is concerning; Multiple Sclerosis typically presents with neurological deficits like weakness or sensory changes rather than isolated unresponsiveness. Did anyone witness the episodes and observe any specific movements like lip-smacking, hand-picking, or bicycling motions of the hands?

REQUEST TEST: Video_EEG_monitoring
REQUEST IMAGES: MRI_Brain

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Interictal spikes and sharp waves localized to the temporal lobes, more prominent on the right side. No evidence of mass lesions, infarctions, or structural abnormalities.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Temporal Lobe Epilepsy. The combination of unresponsiveness with facial grimacing and the specific EEG findings of interictal spikes localized to the right temporal lobe confirms this diagnosis. I will not recommend Multiple Sclerosis given the absence of typical neurological deficits and the clear epileptic activity.
